title: Mucormycosis (Zygomycosis)
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Invasive infection by Mucorales fungi, most often in diabetic ketoacidosis or immunosuppressed patients. Rapid tissue necrosis, angio‑invasion and high mortality demand early recognition and aggressive management.

sections.p: Mucormycosis is a life‑threatening opportunistic fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia). It thrives in high‑glucose, acidic environments and spreads by angio‑invasion, causing tissue infarction.
b: Most common in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hematologic malignancy
Three main clinical forms: rhinocerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous

sections.p: Mucorales are broad, ribbon‑like, non‑septate hyphae that grow rapidly at 30‑37 °C. They produce sporangiospores dispersed in air and soil.
b: Hyphae: 5‑15 µm, irregular width, right‑angle branching
Thermotolerant, thrive in high glucose and iron

sections.p: Spores are inhaled, ingested, or inoculated through skin breaches. In susceptible hosts they germinate, invade blood vessels and spread hematogenously.
b: Environmental exposure: decaying organic matter, compost

sections.p: Clinical presentation depends on portal of entry. Rhinocerebral disease begins with sinus pain, facial swelling and black eschar; pulmonary disease mimics pneumonia; cutaneous disease follows trauma or burns.
b: Rhinocerebral: periorbital edema, ophthalmoplegia, palate necrosis
Pulmonary: fever, cough, hemoptysis, cavitary lesions

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with imaging and tissue confirmation. Histopathology showing broad, non‑septate hyphae with angio‑invasion is diagnostic.

t.b: Localises disease extent; necrotic tissue appears non‑enhancing
Detects characteristic hyphae; rapid bedside test
Elevated iron and uncontrolled diabetes predispose infection

sections.p: Urgent surgical debridement plus systemic antifungal therapy. Reverse underlying metabolic or immunologic abnormalities.
b: First‑line drug: Liposomal amphotericin B – broad Mucorales activity
Posaconazole or isavuconazole for step‑down or intolerance
Control hyperglycaemia, treat ketoacidosis, reduce steroids

sections.p: Focus on risk factors, rapid progression, and the need for combined surgical‑medical therapy.
b: DKA is the classic predisposing condition for rhinocerebral disease
Black necrotic eschar = tissue infarction from angio‑invasion
Amphotericin B is the only drug with proven mortality benefit

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden facial swelling, vision loss, or black eschar in a diabetic patient
Unexplained hemoptysis with fever in an immunocompromised host
Rapid progression of skin necrosis after trauma

faq.q: Why does diabetic ketoacidosis predispose to mucormycosis?
faq.a: Acidosis impairs phagocyte function and high free iron promotes fungal growth.

faq.q: Can a negative culture rule out mucormycosis?
faq.a: No; tissue histology is the gold standard and cultures are often false‑negative.

faq.q: What is the role of iron chelation in treatment?
faq.a: Deferoxamine worsens infection (provides iron to fungi); deferasirox may be adjunctive but is not routine.

exam: A diabetic patient in DKA presents with periorbital swelling and black palate – what is your immediate management? — Recognise rhinocerebral mucormycosis, start liposomal amphotericin B, correct ketoacidosis, arrange urgent ENT debridement.
How does mucormycosis differ from invasive aspergillosis on histology? — Mucorales: broad, non‑septate hyphae with right‑angle branching; Aspergillus: narrow, septate, acute‑angle branching.
Why is voriconazole contraindicated in suspected mucormycosis? — It lacks activity against Mucorales and may allow disease progression.

In a resource‑limited hospital without CT, how would you confirm diagnosis? — Perform bedside KOH prep of sinus or wound tissue; look for broad, ribbon‑like hyphae; proceed to surgical debridement based on clinical picture.
What metabolic correction is essential before antifungal therapy? — Rapid reversal of ketoacidosis and strict glucose control to improve host immunity.

A patient on high‑dose steroids for TB develops pulmonary infiltrates; what clues point to mucormycosis rather than bacterial pneumonia? — Persistent fever despite antibiotics, cavitary lesions with surrounding consolidation, and possible hemoptysis; consider fungal infection.

Explain why surgical debridement is a cornerstone of therapy. — Angio‑invasion causes necrotic tissue that antifungals cannot penetrate; removing dead tissue reduces fungal burden and improves drug delivery.
What are the key prognostic factors influencing mortality? — Delay >6 hours to therapy, extent of disease (disseminated worst), uncontrolled diabetes, and lack of surgical intervention.
